sections.note: Description: In History 100 we will study the world from the eleventh century through the early nineteenth century. This was the first global age, when trade, conquest, and colonization connected all parts of the globe as never before. By 1800, all large areas of human settlement and culture everywhere on earth interacted with one another – some only barely, others in deep and transforming ways. We will focus on three long-term developments that have most powerfully shaped the world in which we live: struggles between colonizers and colonized peoples; the global formation and spread of capitalism; and the process of state and empire formation. We will trace the increasing interconnectivity of people across the globe, the increased inequalities that resulted in oppression, and the constant struggles and resistance from the oppressed. Day1Access course materials cost $63.88. For more information see https://go.illinois.edu/Day1Access.

Title: Black Music Topic: What is black music, and how do we know what we think we know about it? Together, we will examine musical creations pioneered by Africans and individuals of African descent over several centuries and across hemispheres. Doing so will allow us to consider the unity of the African Diaspora and its music, and also examine internal differences and diversity. Special focus is given to the U.S. and Latin America, but we will also read about, listen to, and talk about music and musicians in other parts of the world, especially Asia and Africa. Day1Access course materials cost $6.33 and $10.56. For more information see https://go.illinois.edu/Day1Access.

Topic: Colonial Latin America: Atlantic Encounters, Environments, and Entanglements Description: How did encounters among Indigenous peoples, Africans, and Europeans transform Latin America and the wider world? This course explores colonial Latin America from Atlantic voyages to independence through the movement of people, knowledge, plants, animals, diseases, and commodities. Comparing Spanish and Portuguese America, we examine conquest, slavery, ecological change, race relations, and religious practices. We ask how communities exchanged knowledge, adapted to colonial pressures, and pursued independence. Maps, objects, images, and discussion boards invite students to build knowledge of Latin America through diverse historical media. No previous study of Latin American history is required.

title: Western Worlds: Ancient and Medieval Societies from the Mediterranean to N. Europe (ACP)

sections.note: Advanced Composition Course Description: This course explores the major processes, ideas, and events that formed societies from ancient Mesopotamia to the European colonization of the Americas: over four thousand years of human endeavor. This history influences our everyday lives in fundamental ways; our languages, living spaces, food, clothing, attitudes toward sexuality, political institutions, values, beliefs, basic assumptions - all are rooted in this past. Students will investigate the shared and contested heritage of the West, shaped and reshaped by peoples from the ethnically and culturally diverse regions of western Asia (often called the "Near East" or "Middle East"), North Africa, and Europe. Major themes include the growth and transformation of empires; the emergence and development of Judaism, Christianity, and Islam; the changing status and roles of women; forms of kingship and law; and the impact of new technologies. This course also serves as an introduction to the craft of history, as both an intellectual discipline and a basic human need.

title: Western Worlds: Ancient and Medieval Societies from the Mediterranean to Northern Europe

This course is crosslisted with RLST 120.

Description: This U.S. history survey begins with the diverse peoples who inhabited North America before European contact and extends forward through European colonialism, the movement for independence, the founding of the republic, the Civil War, and Reconstruction, concluding in 1877. The course offers an overview of the region’s history with particular attention to the networks of peoples, ideas, and goods that connected the Atlantic and Pacific worlds, as well as to many forms of social, political, and economic inequality and struggles for freedom and democracy.

Description: This course surveys U.S. history from the end of the Civil War to the recent past. It explores the ways in which people from varied backgrounds experienced the nation’s rise from a primarily agrarian regional power to an industrialized global power. Particular attention is paid to the struggles to achieve a multiracial democracy, the economic and political tensions that arose from industrialization and urbanization, and the intersections between domestic and international affairs. Transformative events are examined from the perspectives of elites who had easy access to the levers of power, activists who fought for change on behalf of traditionally disadvantaged groups, and ordinary Americans who may or may not have been politically active. Students will learn the practice of historical interpretation as they examine documents produced by people from a wide range of backgrounds and perspectives as they endeavored to understand and influence the development of the United States. Day1Access course materials cost $12.81 and $51.75. For more information see https://go.illinois.edu/Day1Access.

Topic: Monarchy, From the Middle Ages to the Present Description:This course will examine the institution of monarchy, specifically in the context of European society, but with consideration to some countries outside of the European continent. This course will analyze why monarchy was, and in many cases remains, a predominant form of societal structuring, how monarchs themselves maintain(ed) power, and how everyday people relate(d) to monarchy. In doing so, we will look at how kingship and queenship changed over the centuries, largely in response to significant movements such as the Enlightenment and nationalism and how, even today, monarchs rule over many countries, albeit largely as figureheads. This course is meant to provide students with an introduction to historical analysis by examining both primary and secondary sources, grappling with key terms and concepts, and the construction of an independent project.

Description: From Alexander the Great and the Roman legions to Napoleon, the World Wars, and the "War on Terror," warfare has transformed states, cultures, technologies, and everyday lives. This section of HIST 200 uses the history of warfare from antiquity to the present as a laboratory for learning how historians think and work. Along the way, we will investigate battles such as Cannae, Agincourt, Borodino, Gettysburg, and Stalingrad while asking bigger questions: Why do wars begin? Why do armies win or lose? How has technology changed warfare? And how have soldiers and civilians experienced—and remembered—war? Students will work with primary sources, confront competing historical interpretations, and learn how to develop research questions, evaluate evidence, and construct persuasive arguments. The course culminates in an independent research project on a topic in military and warfare history chosen by the student.
Title: TBD Description: TBD

Topic: Twentieth Century US Political History Description: This course introduces students to historical interpretation through an examination of the political, social, and cultural changes that occurred in the United States after the New Deal. Emphasis will be given to topics such as the New Deal consensus, postwar prosperity, inequality, the conservative turn, urban renewal, social movements, and partisan politics. Students will also assess historians’ efforts to understand and characterize the unprecedented prosperity the United States experienced after World War II. Over the course of the semester, students will improve their research skills and writing practices as they conduct their own research and produce a final research project.

Title: History of Ancient Greece Topic: The course will examine the political, social, economic, religious, and cultural developments of the Ancient Greek world ca. 3000-30 BCE, from the rise of Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilization to the Roman defeat of Cleopatra.

Topic: The Holocaust in Historical Perspective Description: The purpose of this general education course is to provide students from all backgrounds with an introduction to the complex events in twentieth-century Europe now known as the Holocaust, and to explore the various interpretations that scholars have offered to attempt to explain the Holocaust as well as the global legacy of the Holocaust. We will examine perpetrators, bystanders, and victims, the role of anti-Semitism, the interaction of war and genocide, the relationships between German and other European actors, the responses of Jewish communities, and the memory of the Holocaust. There will be a midterm and a final, but the primary focus of the course will be on student engagement with the texts in two short papers spread out across the semester.

title: History of Medicine in the United States

sections.note: Description: Medicine and public health in the United States from the colonial period through the twentieth century. Topics include medical theories, therapeutic practices, and institutions (medical schools, hospitals, asylums, clinics) and how they have been determined by science, culture, politics, law, and social structures. In addition, we will examine specific diseases and epidemics (including polio, cancer, AIDS); health care providers, patients, and public policy. Throughout, the course highlights race, sex, (dis)ability, and other social categories that have affected medical care (or its lack) and that have been defined in medical terms. The course includes analysis and discussion of original documents, memoirs, art, and film.

Description: This course surveys the African American sociohistorical experience from 1877 to the present. This course examines the interaction between African American's community-building efforts and post-slavery systems of anti-black racial oppression. It surveys transformations of African Americans from sharecropping and apartheid in the South, through migration, urbanization, and proletarianization in the North and West, to contemporary deindustrialization and racialized mass incarceration.

Title: Asian American History Topic: Asian Americans are a dizzyingly diverse group. Most do not even see themselves as "Asian American." How then can we speak of "Asian American history?" What issues arise in trying to incorporate this diversity into one historical narrative, one story? In this course, we will attempt to grapple with this problem. We will relate the activity and the historical circumstances Asian Americans have faced in the United States to the themes of capitalism and democracy, unity and difference that have challenged all Americans. We will examine the reasons why men and women of the Asian continent migrated to what is today the United States, the ways they establish communities and related across generational divides, the challenges of racism, gender, discrimmination, and class exploitation they faced, and the ways they responded to their new conditions. We will explore Asian American history using primary sources, literature, and film as our windows.

Topic: AI in Film and History Description: From the birth of cinema until today, robots and intelligent machines have been a subject of fascination for filmmakers and moviegoers. This class will explore the theme of Artificial Intelligence in film alongside historical developments in computing and social/cultural context. What do these fictional depictions of AI tell us about the times, places, and people who imagined them? And what does it mean if—as some claim—AI is now no longer merely “science fiction”?

Description: The course offers undergraduate students a broad historical survey of immigrants (more broadly, “migrants”) in the United States. It examines recurring themes in migration history, including the global forces shaping migration, the encounters between “natives and strangers,” internal migration, the process of naturalization, race and ethnicity, gender and sexuality, and interethnic relations. Much of the course will center on classroom dialogue and exercises based on lectures, readings, and primary sources. Attendance and informed participation in class discussions are mandatory.

Topic: The Inquisition Description: This course explores the history and legacy of the Inquisition from 1478 to 1834, offering insights into the early modern societies of Iberia and its Latin American colonies. Through trial records, art, literature, and film, students examine how inquisitorial institutions developed, operated, and changed within and beyond Europe. Topics include heresy, witchcraft, and deviancy, alongside debates about “blood purity,” gender, and censorship. Lectures, discussions, and digital labs explore religious authority, tolerance and persecution, and how people defended their beliefs, reputations, and lives. A final project invites students to compare inquisitorial practices across regions or investigate the alleged crimes, practices, and people targeted by the Inquisition.

Topic: The Making of Europe in Prague Description: This is a study abroad course in Prague, Czechia. Tour one of Europe's most beautiful cities and visit locations where history was made: Wenceslas Square, the Jewish Quarter, Prague Castle, the Theresienstadt Ghetto, and the National Opera. Immerse yourself in Czech culture while exploring the region's complex history of ethnic and confessional pluralism, medieval legacies, the rise and fall of empires, and the transformation of European identity. To apply for this course and for additional information, please visit the LAS Study Abroad Website.

Description:This course will focus on the Habsburg Empire, starting with its foundations in the Swiss Alps and the election of the first Habsburg, Rudolf, as King of the Romans. For centuries, the Habsburg dynasty was at the center of European politics, from wars with France and the Ottomans to international expansion into the “New World” and South Asia. We will explore their successes and misfortunes throughout the years while also understanding how this impacts the millions of people within their domains. This includes but is not limited to the marriage diplomacy of Maximilian I, the imperial politics of Charles V’s empire upon which the sun never set, Maria Theresa’s unique perspective as the only woman to officially head the family, and the twilight of the empire under her great-great-grandson Franz Joseph. Throughout all of these moments, we will explore how one family consolidated power and how the diverse peoples of their regimes understood their relationship to that power.

Topic: Shipwrecks Description: The course will explore the culture and politics of shipwreck and castaways from the early modern period to the present day. We will use memoirs and novels to examine how shipwrecks refashion individuals, bind and break society, and create new political worlds of power and freedom. The course will begin with the Cameron’s Titanic (yes, the movie), move back in time and then end with castaways along the Rio Grande River and in the Mediterranean Sea today.

Title: Civil War & Reconstruction Topic: This course begins with a brief investigation of the antebellum period before treating the war years themselves (1861-65). A month is pent strictly on the chronology of the war. This will serve as a good foundation before moving into the books and theme-based discussion that constitutes the heart of the course. This timeline-into-books formula will be repeated for the Reconstruction (1865-77) component of the class. The goal is for students to acquire a deep and comprehensive knowledge of the Civil War and Reconstruction by looking at the era through different and diverse lenses so as to draw the most complete picture possible.

title: US in an Age of Empire

sections.note: Topic: The global backstory to the United States of today, focusing on imperial dimensions of U.S. history from 1877 to 1920. Topics include the imperial world system, global trade and investments, labor migrations, missionary endeavors, civilizing aspirations, consolidation of U.S. power over Native Americans, anticolonial opposition, and U.S. political assertion, military interventions, territorial acquisitions, and colonial governance in places such as Hawaii, Puerto Rico, the Philippines, Guam, the Virgin Islands, Haiti, and the Panama Canal Zone.

Description: This course will examine the creation, maintenance, and transformative patterns of the United States urban space, the Black working class, and capitalism from the Colonial Era to the present day. This course aims to acquaint students with shifting historiographical perspectives, theory, methods, and interpretation in African American urban life and history. Specifically, this class will encourage students to develop their own unique interpretation of existing scholarship and suggest directions for future research. This course will also equip students to deepen their historical perspective on current discussions of African Americans, and the future of the nation. Students will examine the social forces of conflict over space to understand how racial oppression has structured cities since the beginning, including the changing ways legal, economic, spatial, and cultural structures determined how people intentionally underdeveloped cities along social categories like race, class, gender, immigration status, sexuality, or religion.
Meets w/GWS 387 (CRN 63265, Sec. SS)

Description: This course explores the origins and impacts of what historians have termed, “The Rights Revolution.” It encompasses court cases, state and federal legislation, and the changing efforts to enact legal change on everyday people, particularly those relegated to the margins of U.S. society. The course content skips across times and topics: Fourteenth Amendment, Segregation, Voting Restriction, State Anti-Discrimination, and Housing Policy. In addition to racism we look at intersections of sexism, homophobia, ablism, and xenophobia. We consider the context and dynamics of society in the post-Civil War era, World War II, the Cold War, as well as the social movements of black, women’s, and gay rights, and recent legal developments involving anti-immigration and social violence. The course assumes that participants have a strong background in historical studies and that all will commit to joining most class discussions and completing all readings and writing assignments.

Restricted to Students in the History Honors Program. Description: This course does not study the history of any one theme, region, or event. It is rather, a course about the writing of history: what exactly is history? Who and what determines how it is written? What can the particular ways in which the past is preserved, studied, theorized, and memorialized reveal to us not just insights about the past itself, but also about the moment in which history is produced? And how has the interpretation and representation of the past changed over time? Our goal will be to get to grips with responses to these types of questions and to immerse ourselves in some of the key approaches to (and the challenges and pleasures of) historical practice while preparing to write your own work of history, your senior honors thesis.
Restricted to Students in the History Honors Program. Concurrent enrollment in HIST 499 required.

Topic: Empires in Theory and History Description: This course examines the role and significance of empires in history, from the earliest empires in the Fertile Crescent to the collapse of the British Empire in the mid-20th Century. For more than a millennia, empire has been the dominant form of political structuring and students will explore how the system remained in place by examining specific case studies and developing their own research projects. While the case studies will center on European empires, students are invited to focus their own research on any topic related to empire, regardless of geographic or temporal boundaries. As the capstone course for history majors, students will be expected to work both on class material as well as their own research project, utilizing both primary and secondary sources.

Topic: American Sports & Integration Description:The racial integration of Major League Baseball initiated by Jackie Robinson’s 1947 breakthrough has often been labelled a watershed event in U.S. history, mobilizing support for Civil Rights and pushing calls for remaking U.S. society. Yet, those who followed Robinson in professional baseball and in other organized sports discovered the process of pioneering integration was neither swift nor smooth. This research seminar is designed for students willing to think critically about history and undertake research projects about integration in American sports. We analyze questions of historical interpretations by reading “integration stories” through primary and secondary source materials. We engage the experience of pioneering athletes in baseball and other organized sports and also focus on the challenges women athletes encountered as barrier breakers in sports. Seminar assignments include response papers, discussion facilitation, research tasks (i.e. proposal statement, annotated bibliography, rough draft) that culminate in a final research paper (20-25 pages).

Topic: Anti-colonial Resistance in South Asia Description: This course will examine key strands of anti-colonial resistance that developed in modern South Asia during the colonial period. It will assess both elite and subaltern politics by focussing closely on movements and ideologies that responded to the imperial encounter. Students will be encouraged to make connections with present-day politics in the region. By examining the past with an eye to its contemporary relevance, we will explore how anti-colonial mobilisations reshaped modern South Asian cultures.

Topic: Women in the Early Modern World, 1400-1800 Description: In the History 498 capstone seminar, students research and write their own original scholarship. In this section students will focus their work on any aspect of women’s lives in the early modern period, c. 1400-1800. We’ll start by reading about women as wives, widows, witches, domestic workers, craft workers, enslaved workers, nuns, missionaries, leaders, and princes. Students will learn how to locate and interpret works written by women, especially diaries, journals, letters, and memoirs.
Restricted to Honors Senior Thesis Writers in the History Honors Program. Concurrent enrollment in HIST 493 required.

Topic: Writing Regimes: Interrogating Texts and Contexts in Global Perspective Description: Written records are a main source of historical evidence for understanding past societies -- but how should we read, analyze, and critique these texts in order to extract information from them? How can we more fully account for the contextual forces that have shaped a given record, from its material supports (stone, wood, wax, textile, papyrus, parchment, paper) to its entangled and contingent reception history? How have specific documentary regimes worked to control what is preserved and why, and how have modern categories and archiving practices worked to create artificial genres and hierarchies of knowledge? How can we better account for the multiple media (oral, visual, performative) through which texts have been transmitted and accessed – even by non-literate individuals and groups? This seminar will interrogate the making of premodern and modern texts in order to enrich, complicate, and challenge our reliance on them, engaging technologies and practices of literacy from many cultures around the world. Students will then apply what they learn to a particular text or archive relevant to their own research.

Topic: Global Environmental History Description: This graduate-level readings course surveys environmental history from a planetary perspective. We will explore new and classic environmental histories of different places around the globe and place them in comparative and world contexts. With weekly discussions focused on the relations between peoples and their environments, we will aim to survey this dynamic field of historical interpretation while at the same time exploring specific issues such as imperialism and colonialism, indigenous and scientific knowledge, commodification and capitalism, industrialization and pollution, urbanization, environmental justice, and more. While surveying the diverse approaches, topics, and geographies that constitute the field of global environmental history, students will also research and write a state-of-the-field essay about a topic of their choosing.

Topic: Introduction to Digital History Theory and Methods Description: History borrows theory and methods from many disciplines, and the fields of emerging technology and computational analysis are no exception. In Intro to Digital History Theory and Methods, we'll survey the fields of digital and digital public history as we explore how digital history overlaps and diverges from digital humanities and data science in its theoretical and ethical boundaries. We'll also examine how the digitization of primary sources, and the transformation of historical evidence into structured data, shape the historical field in the context of an increasingly data-driven world. The class blends digital-history readings with hands-on encounters in data management and mining, textual analysis, spatial history, networks in historical sources, makerspace reproduction, artificial intelligence, and digital public history. Students will leave the class with basic experience in a wide variety of digital-history and digital-public-history methods and project management skills, demonstrated through the production of a draft grant proposal that includes a working digital-history prototype.

Topic: Living Between Worlds: Women, Migration and the City Description: Living Between Worlds investigates the city as a space of marginal experiences across time and transnational contexts. This seminar probes open-ended ways of rethinking the urban, mainly by foregrounding the experiences of South Asian women in native and diasporic spaces. We experiment with a mix of learning methods that can register embodied, artistic, and archival forms of knowledge. By centering lived experiences from the periphery, this course asks: How do cities accommodate (and erase) women’s labor, mobility, solidarity, and pleasure as spatial practice? In situating South Asian women as subjects, we build on feminist, anti-racist, and post-colonial critiques of dominant, eurocentric ways of imagining urban space.

Description: This graduate seminar examines major themes and historiographical debates in Chinese history from the Neolithic period to 1800. Through critical reading and discussion of secondary sources, students will engage key scholarship and put historical perspectives in conversation with one another. Course topics include the origins of Chinese civilization, political evolution from the pre-imperial to early imperial eras, the Tang-Song transition, intellectual traditions, religions, textual production and manuscript culture, gender and sexuality, ethnicity and conquest dynasties, Chinese law and medicine, and socio-economic and environmental histories.

Description: This course examines the various historiographical approaches to the study of the U.S. during the nineteenth century. In the course we will read a combination of foundational works and new approaches to the long nineteenth century beginning post revolution and ending in the progressive era.

Description: This seminar introduces graduate students to the central contributions and challenges of oral history methods for historical research and writing. We will consider not only how interviews can be used to explore what happened in the past but also how memories of the past are constructed in the present as people make sense of their lives through story and dialogue with others. Topics include: the narrator/interviewer interaction; translation; analysis and interpretation; ethical and legal concerns; digital technology; archiving stories; and intellectual and community responsibility. As part of the course, students will conduct their own oral history interviews.

Description: This seminar for first-year graduate students is the second half of the introductory graduate sequence. It focuses on the process of writing an original piece of historical scholarship. Topics include: developing a research strategy, locating and interpreting sources, engaging with theory and historiography, building an argument, and crafting a polished article-length essay. Students will work with the course instructor and an advisor from their own research field. Prerequisite: HIST 593
